title: Delta-Function Kicks are Optimal for Rapidly Driven Inertial Stochastic Systems
abstract: Optimal control helps guide our understanding of stochastic thermodynamics, leading to universal properties and geometric formulations. Among the initially surprising properties of optimal control, not only discrete jumps but delta function kicks have been shown to be necessary to minimize dissipation in specific example systems. Using a short-time approximation, I show that delta-function kicks are universally optimal for minimizing dissipation in inertial stochastic systems, including active and quantum dynamics under general constraints. Fundamentally stemming from basic kinematics, delta-function kicks are required to achieve linear scaling of work with short protocol durations compared to the quadratic scaling without the kicks. This implies a diverging (infinite) ratio of saved work in the short-time limit.
summary: This work determines the optimal control strategy for rapidly driving inertial stochastic systems to minimize energy dissipation. It proves that delta-function kicks are universally optimal, allowing the saved work to scale linearly with the driving time. This linear scaling represents a significant theoretical improvement over quadratic scaling, providing deep insights into non-equilibrium thermodynamics.
main_problem: The paper investigates the optimal control strategy required to minimize energy dissipation (or maximize saved work) when rapidly driving inertial stochastic systems.
main_result: Optimal control necessitates the application of delta-function kicks, which allows the saved work to scale linearly with the short protocol duration ($\propto \Delta t$), leading to an infinitely large ratio of work savings compared to protocols without kicks.
method: The analysis uses short-time approximations ($\Delta t 	o 0$) applied to the dynamics governed by generalized Langevin equations, optimizing the average work done using impulse control theory.
model_or_system: The system models inertial stochastic dynamics, including active matter and quantum Brownian motion, described by Klein-Kramers dynamics or generalized Langevin equations. The control is implemented via instantaneous momentum shifts (delta-function kicks).

main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the system is inertial and that the optimal control involves impulsive momentum shifts. Specific derivations rely on approximations up to $O(\Delta t^2)$ and assumptions about the dissipator coupling to position.
paper_structure: The paper builds from general optimal control theory in stochastic thermodynamics, applies it to inertial systems using short-time expansions, and compares the performance of delta-function kick protocols against standard linear protocols, showing the superior scaling of the former.
why_interesting: The finding that optimal control requires impulsive kicks to achieve linear work scaling is a powerful, non-intuitive result in non-equilibrium thermodynamics, providing a fundamental constraint on how fast processes can be driven.
